documents.unit: AI at Carleton (Academic AI Advisory Team)
documents.title: Policies - AI at Carleton
documents.stance_why: A coded delegates and B coded permit. The page does not hand the decision to instructors: it states the college's own student rule, that work must be done "in a manner ensuring that the core intellectual substance of the assignment is carried out by the student themselves", and says employees may use Gemini with low and medium risk data. AI use is allowed with conditions, so permit. Faculty are only encouraged to discuss it.
documents.summary: College-wide AI page covering employee data security rules (Gemini only for medium-risk data) and the reworded Academic Integrity policy requiring students to carry out the core intellectual substance of assignments. It does not set a permit or ban for student AI use and leaves how AI fits a course to instructors and students.

units.why: The opening says "Carleton’s existing policies still apply to AI" and that new policies or interpretations may be needed. It frames the institution's approach, so it is a general, informs statement of type P56.
units.resolution_why: Both coders agree on all codes (general, informs, P56): the sentence frames how existing policies apply to AI and that new ones may be needed. Kept A's wording; anchor shortened to the load-bearing clause.
units.anchor: Carleton’s existing policies still apply to AI

units.why: The page states "AI technologies raise novel questions around data security, attribution, and ethics". This is a rationale framing the institution's approach, so it is a general, informs unit of type P56.
units.resolution_why: Only coder A coded this sentence. The source does say "AI technologies raise novel questions around data security, attribution, and ethics", a rationale for the page. It is a real statement of principle, so kept as informs/P56.
units.anchor: AI technologies raise novel questions around data security, attribution, and ethics

units.why: The page promises to "highlight any additions and changes as they’re made". That is the college committing to update its AI policy list, so admin, over-time, informs, P54.
units.resolution_why: Only coder B coded this. The source says the page will "highlight any additions and changes as they’re made", a commitment to keep the AI policy page current. Kept as admin, over-time, P54.
units.anchor: highlight any additions and changes as they’re made
units.frag_start: This page will provide links to
units.policy: The AI policies page highlights additions and changes to AI policies as they are made.

units.why: "Carleton employees should not enter sensitive data or proprietary content into generative AI tools" is a data-protection rule, so should-not, P50, restrict.
units.resolution_why: Both coders agree on all codes. Text is addressed to employees; kept actor all as both coders did.
units.anchor: Carleton employees should not enter sensitive data or proprietary content into generative AI tools

units.why: "The one exception is Google Gemini, which may be used as described below" permits one vetted tool despite the ban on others, so may, P50 (prefer vetted tools), permit.
units.resolution_why: Only coder A split out the Gemini exception; coder B folded the permission into the next unit. The source states a distinct exception rule ("The one exception is Google Gemini"), so kept as its own unit.
units.anchor: The one exception is Google Gemini, which may be used as described below

units.why: Community members are "welcome to submit low and medium risk data" into Gemini through Carleton accounts. It permits use of a vetted tool with data limits: may, P50, permit.
units.resolution_why: Both coders agree on all codes; used B's normalized policy since it follows the passage.
units.anchor: welcome to submit low and medium risk data
units.frag_start: Given these stipulations, Carleton community members
units.policy: Carleton community members are welcome to submit low and medium risk data into Google Gemini when logged in through their Carleton accounts.

units.why: "Under no circumstances should individuals share high risk data" with Gemini is an absolute data-protection ban: must-not, P50, prohibit.
units.resolution_why: A coded should-not, B coded must-not. The source says "Under no circumstances should individuals share high risk data", an absolute bar, so must-not.
units.anchor: Under no circumstances should individuals share
units.frag_start: Under no circumstances should individuals share
units.policy: Under no circumstances should individuals share high risk data (e.g. SSN or credit card information) with Gemini.

units.why: "Before sharing medium risk data with outside vendors, including other generative AI tools... please contact infosec@carleton.edu" is a data-protection step, so should, P50.
units.resolution_why: Both coders agree on all codes. Used B's normalized policy.
units.anchor: Before sharing medium risk data with outside vendors
units.frag_start: Before sharing medium risk data with
units.policy: Before sharing medium risk data with outside vendors, including other generative AI tools, people contact infosec@carleton.edu.

units.why: The page notes Carleton "reworded its Academic Integrity policy to better articulate the guidelines around AI use". It is a statement about the institutional framework, informs, P56.
units.resolution_why: A coded P56/all, B coded P36/admin. The source only reports that Carleton "reworded its Academic Integrity policy to better articulate the guidelines around AI use"; it does not say unauthorized AI use is misconduct, so P36 overreaches. P56 (institution-level framework) fits, and the sentence is addressed to the community, so actor all.
units.anchor: reworded its Academic Integrity policy to better articulate the guidelines around AI use

units.why: Students must complete assignments so that "the core intellectual substance of the assignment is carried out by the student themselves". That limits AI doing the thinking, so must, P32, restrict.
units.resolution_why: A coded P32, B coded P29. The rule that the "core intellectual substance... is carried out by the student themselves" says the student must stay the primary thinker and AI must not replace it, which is P32. P29 (own what you submit) fits the next sentence on responsibility. Both coders agree on actor, phase and modality.
units.anchor: students are expected to complete all assignments
units.policy: Students are expected to complete all assignments in a manner ensuring that the core intellectual substance of the assignment is carried out by the student themselves.

units.why: "The responsibility lies with each student to ensure that they identify and complete" the core substance. This makes students answerable for their work: must, P29.
units.resolution_why: Both coders coded P29, student, during-work, must, neutral. B's unit_stance is neutral as well; the passage allocates responsibility rather than limiting AI.
units.anchor: the responsibility lies with each student to ensure that they identify and complete

units.why: "Faculty are encouraged to discuss this with students" asks instructors to explain what the work is for and how AI helps or hinders learning. It is a communication duty for instructors at the start of the course (should); no existing type covers it, so UNCOVERED.
units.resolution_why: Both coders chose UNCOVERED, should, instructor, course-start; A set unit_stance encourage, B neutral. The passage encourages faculty to talk with students and does not itself encourage or restrict AI use, so neutral. No existing type covers instructors discussing AI rules with students.
units.anchor: faculty are encouraged to discuss this with students
units.policy: Faculty are encouraged to discuss with students, generally and with regard to AI specifically, what the work of their courses is meant to be, how it is meant to benefit their learning, and how AI tools might assist or hinder that learning.
units.uncovered_note: Instructors explain, discuss or word their AI rules for students (rationale, tone, in-class discussion); this is a communication duty not covered by P09 (what must appear in the syllabus) or P41 (why AI shortcuts skill).

documents.unit: Writing Across the Curriculum (Working with AI, resources for faculty)
documents.title: AI Course Policies
documents.stance_why: Both coders: delegates. The page tells faculty "those decisions are ultimately up to you" and links templates that "ban almost all AI use, allow some AI use, and allow all AI use".
documents.summary: Writing Across the Curriculum guidance to faculty on writing course AI policies, with a framework of questions and advice to explain rationale and keep dialogue. It sets no common rule and points to ban, some-use and all-use templates.

units.why: "Start with a working knowledge of what current AI tools can do" advises instructors to learn AI before setting policy: should, P63.
units.resolution_why: Both coders agree on all codes.
units.anchor: Start with a working knowledge of what current AI tools can do

units.why: The page "provides some basic techniques for running your assignment through generative AI tools" so instructors can see how AI affects learning; it supports faculty learning (P63), informs.
units.resolution_why: Only coder A coded this. The source says the page offers techniques for running an assignment through AI tools, which is faculty support, so kept as P63 but modality informs because it describes the page rather than instructing.
units.anchor: techniques for running your assignment through generative AI tools like ChatGPT

units.why: "Seriously consider what writing tasks you want students to do themselves" asks instructors to decide per task what AI may do: should, P04.
units.resolution_why: Both coders agree on all codes.
units.anchor: Seriously consider what writing tasks you want students to do themselves

units.why: The page says telling students "don’t use AI in your writing, period" is not "a practical — or even particularly desirable — solution", advising instructors against a blanket ban: should-not, P04.
units.resolution_why: Both coders agree on actor, phase, modality and type; A coded unit_stance neutral, B permit. The passage advises against a blanket ban, so permit is kept.
units.anchor: that’s not a practical — or even particularly desirable — solution
units.frag_start: So while it may be tempting
units.policy: A blanket ban on AI in student writing is not a practical or particularly desirable solution.

units.why: "some applications of AI can actually help them focus on the most important aspects" says AI can ease ancillary tasks in prose (grammar, citations, proofreading): informs, P18, permit.
units.resolution_why: Both coders agree on all codes.

units.frag_start: Depending on the kinds of intellectual work
units.policy: Some applications of AI can help students focus on the most important aspects of assignments by making ancillary tasks such as grammar, citations and proofreading easier to manage.

units.why: "those decisions are ultimately up to you" leaves it to the instructor whether students practice grammar and similar skills without AI: informs, P04.
units.resolution_why: Both coders agree on all codes. Used B's normalized policy.
units.anchor: those decisions are ultimately up to you
units.frag_start: Of course, you may also decide that you
units.frag_end: those decisions are ultimately up to you.
units.policy: Whether students work on tasks such as grammar, citations and proofreading without AI is up to the instructor.

units.why: "it would be reasonable to allow, or even to explicitly require" AI techniques for some assignments says instructors may allow or require AI, and the decision is theirs: may, P04, permit.
units.resolution_why: A coded may/P02, B coded informs/P04. The passage is about what instructors may decide per course and assignment, not a default for all courses, so P04 fits and P02 (default rule) does not. "Reasonable to allow" grants permission to instructors, so may.
units.anchor: it would be reasonable to allow, or even to explicitly
units.frag_start: it’s also fairly easy to imagine
units.policy: In some courses and assignments it is reasonable for the instructor to allow, or even to explicitly require, students to use some AI techniques; the decision is the instructor's.

units.why: "Set clear guidelines for your students and explain the rationale behind them" tells instructors to set clear AI rules and say why: should. No existing type covers explaining and setting out rationale, so UNCOVERED.
units.resolution_why: A coded UNCOVERED, B coded P41. P41 is about AI shortcutting skill-building practice; this passage is a general duty to set clear guidelines and explain their rationale, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Set clear guidelines for your students
units.frag_start: Set clear guidelines for your students
units.policy: Instructors set clear AI guidelines for students and explain the rationale behind them, including why certain uses of AI would undermine the value of the course or assignments for them.
units.uncovered_note: Instructors explain, discuss or word their AI rules for students (rationale, tone, in-class discussion); this is a communication duty not covered by P09 (what must appear in the syllabus) or P41 (why AI shortcuts skill).

units.frag_start: State your AI policies clearly on the syllabus
units.policy: State your AI policies clearly on the syllabus.

units.resolution_why: A coded P09, B coded UNCOVERED; phase A course-start, B before-course. P09 is the requirement to include an AI statement; this passage is advice on how to word it, so UNCOVERED. Communicating a statement in the syllabus is course-start.

units.anchor: a complete policy would address
units.policy: A complete AI policy addresses how students are permitted to use AI and what uses are explicitly forbidden.

The passage requires that assignments with different rules carry their own AI statement, which is P09 (AI statement in assignment instructions) not the let-instructors-decide rule. "You'll also need to" is must; communicating, so course-start.
units.anchor: you’ll also need to write clear AI policies for any assignment that deviates
units.frag_start: Will the rules around AI vary from one assignment

units.anchor: be prepared to spend some time discussing them in class
units.frag_start: Finally, regardless of the policies you set
units.policy: Instructors discuss their AI policies in class, addressing them by the time students begin the first major writing assignment, explaining the logic and giving students a chance to respond and ask questions.

units.resolution_why: Both coders agree on all codes. Topics merged from both coders.

units.anchor: we will increasingly need to trust our students to follow our policies voluntarily
units.policy: Instructors will increasingly need to trust students to follow AI policies voluntarily, since prohibitions may be unenforceable in practice.

units.policy: Instructors maintain an open dialogue and encourage students to come to them with questions about AI tools and how to use them in the course.

units.why: "using AI to generate text or perfect their grammar diminish students’ learning" asks instructors to explain how such uses undermine learning: should, P41.

units.anchor: using AI to generate text or perfect their grammar diminish students’ learning
units.policy: Instructors explain how using AI to generate text or perfect grammar would diminish students' learning or undermine the benefits of completing the assignments without these tools.

units.frag_start: What limitations of AI tools should they be aware of

new_types.name: Instructors discuss and explain AI rules with students
new_types.definition: Instructors set out, explain and discuss their AI rules and rationale with students (tone of statements, in-class discussion, purpose of assignments, open dialogue). Distinct from P09 (what must appear in syllabi) and P41 (why AI shortcuts skill).

notes: Documents: Carleton AI policies page (university) and Writing Across the Curriculum AI course policies guide (university-layer faculty advice). No school or computing documents. Seven units are UNCOVERED, all about instructors explaining or discussing AI rules with students; proposed as one new type. Doc 1 stance was resolved to permit (A delegates, B permit). A repeated Key Ideas bullet on reiterating policies on assignment prompts was dropped as a repeat of the later detailed passage.
